analysis.one_liner: Bans large-mesh drift gillnets off U.S. coasts and pays fishermen to switch to cleaner gear.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate committee approved the phase-out and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never held a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Drift gillnets are mile-long nets that drift in the ocean and catch fish by their gills; anything else caught in them — whales, dolphins, sea turtles, sharks — is discarded dead or dying. Current law only bans nets 2.5 kilometers or longer. This bill would also ban nets with very large mesh (14 inches or more), which is the type used by a small fleet of West Coast swordfish boats. It would buy back permits from fishermen who give up the nets, pay for the surrender of their gear, and fund a switch to fishing methods that rarely catch protected animals. The Senate Commerce Committee approved it, but the full Senate never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: The public gets healthier oceans: fewer whales, dolphins, sea turtles, and sharks killed as unintended catch off the U.S. coast. Swordfish fishermen willing to switch to more selective gear get government grants to buy back their permits and replace their nets. Fishermen who stay in the fishery under alternative gear benefit from a cleaner-sounding, more marketable product.

how_it_helps.text: Expands the definition of banned large-scale driftnet fishing to include gillnets with a mesh size of 14 inches or greater, the type responsible for entanglement and mortality of protected marine species off the West Coast [S2][S3].

Creates a transition program run by the Department of Commerce that pays fishermen to permanently surrender their driftnet permits, forfeit their nets, and buy alternative gear with minimal incidental catch — payments are allowed only after the permit is permanently revoked and no new ones will be issued [S2][S3].
Makes phase-out of large-mesh driftnet fishing an explicit national policy and directs promotion of fishing methods that minimize accidental catch of living marine resources [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The small fleet of West Coast drift gillnet fishermen loses its current way of fishing, softened by permit buyback and gear-replacement grants. Taxpayers fund the transition program. Swordfish prices may rise slightly as supply shifts to other methods.

drawbacks.text: The committee-reported version softens the ban: it allows driftnet fishing with large-mesh nets shorter than 2.5 kilometers to continue for up to 5 years after enactment, so entanglement of whales and turtles would continue during the phase-out window [S3].

The buyout grants only cover permit fees, forfeited gear, and replacement gear — they do not compensate fishermen for the lost future income from a fishery they would have to leave, so some boat owners could end up worse off even with transition money [S3].

Funding for the transition program is modest and the grant mechanism depends on a separate provision of existing law, which supporters acknowledge could leave the transition underfunded relative to the number of permits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a small, well-documented source of harm: nets that indiscriminately kill protected ocean animals as a routine cost of doing business. The cost falls on a very small number of fishing businesses, and the bill pays them to exit or convert rather than just banning them outright. The main honest criticism is design, not intent — the five-year window the committee added lets the harm continue, and the buyouts may not fully make fishermen whole.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's list of pending business in December 2018, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill in April 2018 with bipartisan cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee [S5].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on September 5, 2018 [S5].

On December 11, 2018, the committee reported the bill to the full Senate, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 729 — meaning it was waiting for floor time [S5][S3].
No vote ever occurred on the Senate floor, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The handful of drift gillnet fishing operations kept their permits and could keep fishing with large-mesh nets for the indefinite future, and the fishermen willing to exit got no buyout. Whales, dolphins, and turtles off the West Coast gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The drift gillnet fleet kept fishing

sides.party_line_note: There was no visible partisan fight: a Democratic sponsor introduced it with two Democratic and two Republican cosponsors, and the Republican committee chair reported it favorably; it died only because the full Senate never scheduled a vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The fleet's catch method routinely entangles whales, dolphins, sea turtles, and sharks as unintended catch; the bill bans that method, with buyback payments to leave the fishery and grants to switch to selective gear. Without the bill, the fleet keeps operating as before [S2][S3].
Transition grants can be used to purchase alternative gear with minimal incidental catch, creating a small new market for makers of that equipment while helping reduce harm to ocean wildlife [S3].
